entries.title: Armed men kidnap dozens in attacks on Nigerian villages
entries.summary: Police say three villages and a mosque were attacked, and worshippers kidnapped in central Niger State.
entries.content:
Police say three villages and a mosque were attacked, and worshippers kidnapped in central Niger State.

Armed men have kidnapped dozens of people during an attack on a mosque and surrounding villages in Nigeria’s central Niger State, survivors and police officials say.

The raiders stormed Kpenya Mosque in the Dekara district of Borgu Local Government Area at around 2pm (13:00 GMT) on Friday, after first attacking the villages of Gidan-Zana and Kpenya, police spokesperson Wasiu Abiodun said on Saturday.

Recommended Stories

list of 3 items
  • list 1 of 3Nigeria’s election campaign begins with Tinubu facing a reform test
  • list 2 of 3Death toll from Nigeria boat accident rises to at least 52
  • list 3 of 3Nigeria and the Sahel: A growing security divide

Abiodun told the Reuters news agency that police were aware of the kidnappings but had not received reports of anyone being killed, and that a “joint security detachment has been deployed to the area for assessment and rescue operations”.

He said police could not yet confirm the number of people who were taken.

Local residents told Reuters that more than 60 worshippers were kidnapped, but the figure could not be independently verified.

Separately, residents told the AFP news agency that people were also killed, another claim that could not immediately be confirmed.

Jibril Ahmad, a survivor of the assault on Dekara, blamed members of the Lakurawa armed group.

“Soon after finishing the normal Friday prayer, the armed group of Lakurawa, in their hundreds, wielding guns, knives and machetes, began to attack us,” Ahmad told AFP, claiming that people were “slaughtered”.

During the attack, a third group, Mahmuda, intervened and clashed with the kidnappers, allowing some abductees to escape, he said.

Federal lawmaker Jafaru Mohammed told AFP that several nearby villages were also struck.

“Some members of the Mahmuda group were against the doctrine of the Lakurawa, and when they heard of what the Lakurawa were doing, they fought them,” Mohammed said.

The attack unfolded in a region near Nigeria’s western border with Benin that has seen growing activity from local armed groups and fighters from the neighbouring region, even as the country’s 17-year armed rebellion remains concentrated in the northeast.

The violence in Niger State continued into Saturday. Resident Abdullahi Ahmad said the group returned to the area to seize more people as a “bargaining chip” in advance of an expected troop deployment, and planted landmines on the road out of Dekara.

“A man and his family who were fleeing the town yesterday were killed when their car hit a landmine planted by the terrorists. Everyone is living in fear,” he said.

Mass abductions have been a hallmark tactic of the country’s armed groups and have evolved into a lucrative, multimillion-dollar industry involving networks of both ideological and nonideological gangs across Nigeria’s northwest and central regions.

entries.title: Trump seeks to block the BBC’s attempt to subpoena Ivanka Trump, Trump Jr
entries.summary: While lawyers for the US president argue the subpoenas are 'cynical', the BBC says they could help shine light on case.
entries.content:
While lawyers for the US president argue the subpoenas are ‘cynical’, the BBC says they could help shine light on a $10bn defamation case.

United States President Donald Trump has called on a federal court to deny a motion by the BBC to subpoena members of his immediate family, as part of a $10bn lawsuit over a documentary the broadcaster aired.

On Friday, lawyers for Trump argued that the BBC had embarked on a “politically charged discovery campaign” by seeking to compel testimony from Trump’s eldest son Donald Trump Jr, his first daughter Ivanka Trump and his son-in-law Jared Kushner.

Recommended Stories

list of 3 items
  • list 1 of 3Editor of US newspaper Stars and Stripes reportedly fired under Trump
  • list 2 of 3Trump administration subpoenas New York Times reporters over coverage
  • list 3 of 3ABC News says FCC is carrying out intimidation campaign to shape coverage

Trump’s team appealed to the court to reject the BBC’s motion, comparing it to a fishing expedition that goes beyond the scope of the case.

“This case concerns a narrow wrong — the BBC’s deliberate splicing together of two passages of President Trump’s January 6, 2021, speech spoken nearly fifty-five minutes apart,” Friday’s court filing said.

“Rather than litigate that narrow claim, the BBC has attempted to pursue a sweeping investigation disguised as discovery.”

The case began in December, when Trump announced he would sue the BBC over an episode of the documentary series Panorama, which chronicled the Republican leader’s path to a second term as president.

Part of the documentary focuses on the events of January 6, 2021, the day the results of the 2020 election were to be certified. Trump had lost that election but falsely claimed his defeat was the result of fraud.

At a speech in front of the White House on that day, he repeated the unfounded accusation that the election had been “rigged” to a rally of his supporters, some of whom participated in an attack on the US Capitol in the hours afterwards.

The Panorama episode included snippets from Trump’s speech, and critics argued that two sentences from his address had been edited together to sound like one continuous quote.

The first line was: “After this, we’re going to walk down, and I’ll be there with you, we’re going to walk down.” The second came from later in the speech: “And we fight. We fight like hell.”

Though the BBC apologised for the editing and took the Panorama episode down from its platforms, Trump nevertheless filed a multibillion-dollar lawsuit accusing the broadcaster of defamation.

The BBC has denied that charge and pledged to fight the lawsuit in court. The case is currently being heard before the US district court in southern Florida.

As part of its defence, the BBC has sought testimony from figures close to Trump, to establish his thoughts and actions on the day of the January 6 attack.

It pointed out that both Donald Trump Jr and Ivanka Trump were present at their father’s speech, and that they spoke to the president and his inner circle as the violence erupted at the Capitol.

Text messages released by the US Congress show Donald Trump Jr urged his father’s chief of staff to “condemn this shit. Asap”, a fact cited in the BBC’s motion.

While Kushner was not present at the White House, the BBC maintains that his role as Trump’s adviser would also help establish the facts of that day.

Lawyers for the broadcaster say that, after speaking with congressional leaders, Kushner drafted “a proposed statement” for Trump to present, “which would have condemned the use of violence”.

The testimony of Trump Jr, Ivanka Trump and Kushner can help illustrate the president’s “burden to prove that it would be materially false to imply that he incited violence on January 6”, according to the BBC’s motion.

But, the motion added, the BBC has been unable to serve the three family members with subpoenas due to the presence of their US Secret Service protection.

The BBC reportedly attempted to deliver subpoenas to Ivanka Trump and Kushner at their residence in May, only to face Secret Service agents who said they were not authorised to accept the documents.

Likewise, that same month, the BBC was unable to hand Trump Jr a subpoena at Trump Tower in New York. It has therefore asked the court for permission to use certified mail to deliver the documents instead.

But in Friday’s court filing, Trump’s lawyers accused the BBC of carrying out a “cynical” campaign that involved the “harassment of the President’s family, associates, staff, officials, and others”.

It also called the BBC’s efforts “a boundless re-investigation of the events that occurred on January 6, 2021”.

The filing suggests that any interactions involving Ivanka Trump and Kushner are “subject to the executive privilege” of the presidency, since the husband-wife duo served as adviser and senior adviser to Trump, respectively.

Trump has made sweeping claims to executive privilege throughout his two terms in office.

Just this month, the US Department of Justice issued a memo saying such privilege shielded communication even with private advisers who worked outside the executive branch, effectively declaring interactions with companies and private individuals off-limits for subpoenas.

Critics fear the memo will be a hurdle to government transparency under Trump — and may even prevent Congress from accessing investigative materials.

Senator Adam Schiff of California framed the memo as an insurance policy against congressional oversight, should the Republican Party lose its majorities in Congress during November’s midterm elections.

“This latest opinion should be seen as a partisan measure to insulate the president and his corrupt activities from Congressional subpoenas when the majority flips,” he wrote in a statement on August 11.

The federal court in southern Florida has yet to rule on the BBC’s subpoena requests.

The BBC, meanwhile, has sought to have the entire case tossed, on the basis that Trump is attempting to dampen free speech.

entries.title: ‘Not a small issue’: People deported by US to Liberia face uncertain future
entries.summary: Liberia's government announced the move on Tuesday, two days before the flight. Politicians say they were not consulted.
entries.content:
The Liberian government announced the move on Tuesday, two days before the flight. But politicians say they were not consulted.

Monrovia, Liberia – Samwar Fallah began receiving calls this week from people in the United States seeking information about 20 relatives sent to Liberia, a country none of them is a citizen of.

The families asked the Monrovia-based lawyer to find out where their relatives were taken and what would happen to them. He could not tell them much.

Recommended Stories

list of 4 items
  • list 1 of 4First group of US deportees, out of an expected 1,200, arrive in Liberia
  • list 2 of 4Liberia to take 1,200 deportees from the US
  • list 3 of 4Liberia’s kush crisis: The hidden trade behind a generation at risk
  • list 4 of 4From palava huts to TikTok: How Liberians are preserving their past

He knows the group landed at Roberts International Airport near capital Monrovia on Thursday and was driven away in a bus by Liberian officials. He does not know where they were taken, whether they are free to leave, or what legal status they now hold.

Fallah avoids calling them deportees because the government has not defined their status under Liberian law.

“You cannot relocate a citizen from one country to another without clear information as to why that person has been relocated,” Fallah told Al Jazeera. “Imagine you coming from maybe El Salvador and then you find out you are on a plane to Liberia.”

The group is the first transferred under an arrangement allowing Liberia to receive up to 1,200 people deported from the US over the next 12 months.

The Liberian government announced the move on Tuesday, two days before the flight. Politicians say they were not consulted.

Fallah, assisting the families without charge alongside two US immigration lawyers, said they want to know whether their relatives may settle in Liberia, choose where they can go, or eventually return to the US.

He has no answers.

The arrangement involves third-country deportation: sending people to a country other than their country of citizenship. It has raised questions about executive power, sovereignty and the rights of those transferred.

‘Guests of the Republic’

The government said the deportees have not been detained and described the arrangement with the US as humanitarian.

Information Minister Jerolinmek Piah said those transferred would be received as “guests of the Republic”. They are free to leave and may seek asylum, he added.

Piah linked the decision to Liberia’s history as a settlement for free and formerly enslaved Black people from the US and a country whose citizens sought protection abroad during 14 years of civil war.

“Liberia’s gesture is entirely humanitarian and in keeping with the country’s longstanding traditions,” he said.

Piah insisted Liberia would not bear the cost. Accommodation, food and eventual onward travel would be covered by the US government and an international partner organisation, he said.

However, the government has not provided further information about the people who arrived on Thursday. It has not disclosed their full nationalities, where they are being housed, the legal documents under which they entered Liberia, or the identity of the international organisation paying for and managing their stay.

The Reuters news agency on Friday reported that five of those people refused to leave the plane and were instead transported to Equatorial Guinea. Al Jazeera has not verified the report independently.

Justice Minister Natu Oswald Tweh said Liberia reviews each passenger list and may reject anyone. “Most of them are people who had immigration violations and offences,” he said.

But the government has not published its screening criteria or said whether any arrivals had US protection orders preventing their return to their countries.

Al Jazeera found out that most of those deported were nationals of Latin American countries, including Venezuela and Cuba.

But “guests” does not establish a legal status under Liberian law. It remains unclear whether those people entered on temporary permits, whether they can work, or whether they must apply for asylum or residency.

Although Piah said the group was free to leave, officials did not allow journalists to speak with them at the airport. They walked down the aircraft steps, boarded a bus and were driven away under official supervision.

Was legislative approval required?

Some of the strongest objections came from politicians who say the arrangement may require legislative approval.

Nimba County Senator Samuel Kogar cited Article 57 of Liberia’s constitution, which empowers the president to conduct foreign affairs and conclude treaties, conventions and similar agreements “with the concurrence of a majority of each House of the Legislature”.

“Was this arrangement brought before both Houses of the Legislature and approved by the required majority?” Kogar asked. “If not, then under what legal authority was this agreement made?”

The government said the arrangement rests on diplomatic notes exchanged on September 4 and September 10 last year.

Third Country Deportation Watch, a project operated by Refugees International and Human Rights First, said the text appeared on the US State Department’s website in March. Most Liberians heard about it only in August.

Representative Anthony F Williams, a member of House committees covering national security, human rights and foreign affairs, rejected the idea that the executive could act alone.

“No agreement that borders on the national security of this country, the sovereignty of the country, can just be entered into by the executive branch alone,” he told Al Jazeera.

The legislature is on a break until October. Williams said he would seek answers on housing, healthcare, screening and Liberia’s authority to detain or remove anyone.

His concerns, he said, were about state capacity, not the arrivals.

Liberia lacks the biometric systems and trained personnel to document as many as 1,200 people moving across counties or porous borders, he said, adding that those fleeing persecution could also be traced by the governments they escaped.

Eddie Jarwolo, executive director of NAYMOTE Partners for Democratic Development, said no published plan showed how Liberia would accommodate the arrivals without further straining public services.

Civil society groups were not consulted, he said. He called for independent monitoring of living conditions, spending and legal compliance.

Was there a diplomatic tradeoff?

The government insists Liberia received no payment or diplomatic reward for accepting the transfers. Critics have called for disclosure of the negotiations.

The arrangement emerged amid several US decisions affecting Liberia. On December 9, 2025, the countries signed a five-year, $124m health memorandum. Washington also extended B1/B2 visitor visas for Liberians from 12 to 36 months.

Al Jazeera previously reported that those measures followed Liberia’s agreement to accept Kilmar Abrego Garcia, whose mistaken removal from the US to a Salvadoran prison became a political and legal flashpoint.

The US later sought court permission to send him to Liberia.

Meanwhile, migrant visas for Liberians were halted in January, according to Third Country Deportation Watch, and the US awarded Liberia $5m this year for migration management.

Neither government has publicly established a direct link between the deportation arrangement and the visa move. Jarwolo of NAYMOTE said the two nations should disclose whether visa extension was linked to accepting third-country deportees.

“If they were linked, it would raise serious concerns about Liberia’s negotiating position, national sovereignty and public safety,” he said. “Development assistance should not require Liberia to accept individuals whose backgrounds and legal status have not been transparently disclosed and properly assessed.”

University of Liberia Student Union president William Sando said he learned of the arrangement through Facebook before Piah confirmed it.

“They have not adequately informed the Liberian people,” he said, rejecting the minister’s argument as “disconnected from the current reality”.

Sando wanted the government to disclose where the arrivals will live and whether those who remain may work.

Kogar, the senator, said the questions went beyond an opposition to migration.

“This is not a small issue,” he said. “We are talking about our sovereignty, our laws, our national security, and the responsibility we have to the Liberian people. Where are we, the Liberians?”

entries.title: Seven killed, including two police officers, in UK ‘wrong-side’ car crash
entries.summary: Accident follows similar crashes in Ireland where police highlighted social media trend driving in opposite direction.
entries.content:
Accident follows two similar crashes in Ireland where police highlighted a social media trend of driving in the opposite direction.

Seven people, including two police officers, have died in a head-on collision during a pursuit, after a vehicle driving down the wrong side of a major road hit a police car in the United Kingdom.

All occupants of both vehicles were pronounced dead at the scene near Middlesbrough in northeast England on Saturday, according to the Cleveland Police.

Recommended Stories

list of 3 items
  • list 1 of 3Landmark trial on Meta’s impact on children’s mental health begins in US
  • list 2 of 3Four killed in helicopter crash in Brazil’s Rio de Janeiro
  • list 3 of 3Singapore-flagged container ship crashes into riverbank in India

A total of 12 people have been killed in less than a week in separate accidents involving cars driving on the wrong side of the road in the UK and Ireland, as a similar collision occurred in Dublin on Sunday.

The Cleveland Police said five members of the public were travelling along the wrong side of the road in a Volkswagen Passat when it collided with a marked police vehicle heading in the correct direction at around 3:39am (02:39 GMT).

Authorities are investigating the exact circumstances of the crash but said they understood that officers had begun a pursuit when they sighted a “suspicious vehicle”.

“This is an incredibly sad day for Cleveland,” Cleveland Police Chief Constable Victoria Fuller said.

The police force said it had formally identified the passengers in the Volkswagen Passat and was contacting their families.

Fuller named the two dead officers as police constables Matthew ⁠Blades, 37, and Tom Clough, 38, describing ⁠them as “brave officers … who didn’t return home to their families at the end of their shift”.

UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham said on X that he was “devastated” to hear about the loss of life and urged people “to avoid speculation at this time”.

The incident follows two similar recent head-on crashes near Dublin, with authorities there highlighting a social media-driven trend for “wrong-side” driving among young people.

After the collision in Dublin on Sunday, Ireland’s prime minister, or taoiseach, Michael Martin, said it was the latest in a series of similar incidents. “There can be no tolerance for this reckless behaviour that we have seen on our roads recently. It must stop,” Martin said.

Irish police chief Justin Kelly added that it came after another head-on crash on a motorway and warned that “what makes this reckless behaviour even more appalling is that in some cases it is being done for social media”.

An Irish parliament committee has asked short-form video platform TikTok to explain how it removes content “that appears to glorify dangerous ‌and ‌illegal behaviour on our roads”. On Tuesday, Ireland’s media regulator made a similar request.

entries.title: South Korea sending first container ship through Arctic route
entries.summary: PanStar Acro, bound for Europe via Arctic, is testing whether a route opened by melting sea ice is commercially viable.
entries.content:
The PanStar Acro, bound for Europe via the Arctic, is testing whether a route opened by melting sea ice can be commercially viable.

A South ‌Korean container ship is sailing to Europe via the Arctic, ⁠in the nation’s first commercial voyage on the route to test its viability as the war in the Middle East rattles global shipping.

The PanStar Acro set sail from Busan New Port on Saturday. “We would like to inform you that the vessel for the Arctic route trial voyage departed” at 9:30pm (12:30 GMT), Seoul’s Ministry of Oceans and Fisheries said in a statement to the AFP news agency.

Recommended Stories

list of 4 items
  • list 1 of 4South Korea footballers urge safety after extreme heat statistics
  • list 2 of 4Putin warns of tit-for-tat seizures of European vessels
  • list 3 of 4Activists’ bid to sue Russia over climate change gets off to shaky start
  • list 4 of 4Can China’s new Arctic sea route to Europe replace Middle East chokepoints?

The PanStar Acro will sail north, the Reuters news agency reported, hugging eastern Russia’s Kamchatka Peninsula, then cross the Bering Sea, and ⁠take the Northern Sea Route, stopping in Felixstowe in the UK, Rotterdam in the Netherlands, and Poland’s Gdansk before returning.

The 2,758 TEU (twenty-foot equivalent unit) container ship operated by South Korea’s PanStar ‌has secured 837 TEU of cargo, including car parts, chemical products and about 100 empty containers on the government-backed voyage.

The journey is expected to take 40 to 45 days, according to the Oceans Ministry.

President Lee Jae Myung has made Arctic shipping ‌a priority for South Korea, with the hope of turning the southeastern ⁠port of Busan into a global maritime hub and position the Arctic as a regular trade route by 2030.

But this new route has been criticised for several different reasons. Environmental groups have warned the route could accelerate polar ice melt, meaning the increase in shipping could worsen global warming.

The project also risks increasing friction with Western allies hoping to keep Russia isolated in its war with Ukraine. Seoul has consulted with Moscow about the journey, Reuters reported, including whether the ship needed ⁠help to tackle any problems, such as ⁠getting stuck in ice.

Last year, 103 transits through the route were made by 88 vessels, up from ⁠97 in 2024 and 43 in 2022, chiefly from nations such as Russia and China, according ⁠to Norway’s Centre for High North Logistics.

But with the Iran war affecting global shipping, governments and shipping firms are scrambling to seek different routes, with the Arctic route increasingly viewed as a viable alternative due to technological advances and environmental degradation.

South Korea’s Vice Oceans Minister Nam Jae-hon said the Arctic route was “bound to become an alternative” to Middle Eastern shipping lanes.

The usual maritime route between Asia and Europe runs through the Suez Canal, but travelling through the Arctic can cut the journey by approximately 7,000 kilometres (4,300 miles) and about 10 days, according to the Korea Institute for International Economic Policy.

However, major carriers including CMA CGM, MSC and Hapag-Lloyd have pledged to avoid Arctic shipping routes due to pressure from environmental groups. The Arctic sea route is believed to be accessible only during the time of year when the ice is melted enough to allow transits without icebreakers.

“The Northern Sea Route has become increasingly viable as the Arctic warms about four times faster than the global average, leading to a sharp decline in sea ice,” South Korean environmental group Paran Ocean Citizen Science Center said in a statement last year. “But making the route commercially viable would require further warming, putting the policy at odds with efforts to combat climate change.”

entries.title: Elche vs Barcelona: La Liga – prediction, team news, lineups
entries.summary: Barcelona start their season at Elche in La Liga on Sunday but will do so without their new signing, Rodri.
entries.content:
Barcelona start their season at Elche in La Liga on Sunday but will do so without their new signing, Rodri.

Who: Elche vs Barcelona

What: Spanish football’s La Liga

Where: Manuel Martinez Valero Stadium, Elche, Spain

When: Sunday, August 23, at 9:30pm (19:30 GMT)

How to follow: Al Jazeera Sport will bring you all the build-up from 16:30 GMT ahead of our live text commentary stream

Hansi Flick’s second season at Barcelona built on the success of his first, with the German coach guiding the Catalan giants to a second straight La Liga title.

Recommended Stories

list of 4 items
  • list 1 of 4Man Utd humiliated at Hull to open Premier League account
  • list 2 of 4Fans and police injured in pitch invasion during ‘high risk’ German Cup tie
  • list 3 of 4Usain Bolt’s 100m record broken at World Humanoid Robot Games
  • list 4 of 4Former world champion boxer Zolani Tete shot and killed in South Africa

His third campaign, however, brings significant structural changes to the team as Barcelona look to maintain their domestic dominance and handle the threat of Jose Mourinho’s Real Madrid, while aiming to end their wait for Champions League glory.

Barca begin their campaign at Elche on Sunday in the Spanish top flight, a day after Mourinho’s Los Blancos visit Espanyol in the Catalan capital.

Al Jazeera Sport takes a closer look at the start of the La Liga defence.

What changes have Barcelona made?

The arrival of Rodri from Manchester City is Barca’s most significant addition, while the departures of veteran striker Robert Lewandowski and Ferran Torres leave Flick with a reshaped attacking unit.

Barcelona have been prolific going forward but vulnerable at the back since Flick arrived in 2024, and the club hopes the arrival of World Cup winner Rodri can help address the latter.

The Spain captain was a market opportunity Barcelona were reluctant to pass up, particularly with Real Madrid also linked with the 30-year-old holding midfielder before his move to Catalonia.

Rodri brings not only control and defensive protection but also the experience of winning the biggest trophies in club football, qualities Barcelona hope can help them claim a first European crown since 2015.

“I’m here to compete for everything, for big things like the Champions League,” said Rodri after his presentation.

Former Germany and Bayern boss Flick will also have to rebuild an attack that has been one of the team’s greatest strengths.

New arrivals Anthony Gordon and Karim Adeyemi appear well-suited to the German’s high-intensity approach, with both offering the pace and work rate required to lead Barcelona’s aggressive pressing game.

How will Barcelona solve their case of the missing striker?

The key question for Barcelona is whether sporting director Deco can land a centre-forward before the transfer window closes.

Barca’s attempt to sign Julian Alvarez splintered on the rocks of Atletico Madrid’s resolve, leaving Flick without an obvious replacement for Lewandowski.

“What Ferran did we can cover with the signings, but what Robert did is more difficult,” said Deco.

“We have internal solutions, but we will make another move; we’ll try and find the best solution.”

Barcelona could opt for a cheaper attacker and preserve their spending power for next summer, particularly after making pricey moves for Rodri and Gordon.

Dani Olmo, Raphinha, Gordon and Adeyemi can all operate as false nines, giving Flick different ways to compensate for the absence of a traditional striker, if the club does not get a deal over the line.

Above all, Barcelona will hope teenage sensation Lamine Yamal can remain in his extraordinary form and enjoy a full season at the top of his game after injuries and other concerns disrupted the early months of his previous campaign.

At just 19, Yamal is already the crucial figure in Barcelona’s attack and the player around whom the club’s ambitions are built.

If Rodri can provide greater stability behind him and Flick finds enough goals across a reshaped attack, Barcelona have the tools they need to retain their Liga crown.

Flick did not reveal who would start up front at Elche but praised the preseason form of Egyptian youngster Hamza Abdelkarim, after the 18-year-old notched four goals in friendlies.

“Hamza is having a really great preseason,” said Flick.

“He’s a number nine, he’s young, and he has a lot of potential, and also he scored goals. This is the important thing when you’re playing in this position, and he made a great job.”

What happened the last time Elche played Barcelona?

Barcelona won 3-1 at the Martinez Valero in La Liga in January, with Yamal, Ferran Torres and Marcus Rashford scoring for the visitors.

Prediction

The Opta supercomputer makes Barcelona strong favourites, giving Hansi Flick’s side a 68 percent chance of winning, compared with 14 percent for Elche.

Head-to-head

This will be the 57th competitive meeting between the clubs. Barcelona have won 36 of the previous encounters, with Elche winning on nine occasions.

Elche team news

Elche will be without Adam Boayar and Yago Santiago due to injury.

Martin Anselmi’s side drew 1-1 with Deportivo on the opening weekend and are expected to retain a three-man defence against Barca.

Elche predicted starting lineup

Dituro; Chust, Redondo, Affengruber; Sangare, Villar, Aguado, Valera; Houary, Nino, Cepeda

Barcelona team news

Rodri will miss the match, but the former Manchester City midfielder may be able to take part in their second match, against Athletic Bilbao, on Thursday.

“He’s very concentrated, focused. Our plan is that he will arrive on Monday with the team,” Flick told reporters on Saturday.

Frenkie de Jong remains out, while Roony Bardghji is also unavailable due to a cruciate ligament injury.

Flick, however, said full-back Joao Cancelo, signed this week, could feature.

“He’s ready to play. He has unbelievable technique and a lot of passion,” added Flick.

Barcelona predicted starting lineup

J Garcia; E Garcia, Kounde, Martin, Balde; Pedri, Bernal; Yamal, Fermin, Raphinha; Abdelkarim
